newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey attacks Kurd rebels in Iraq despite protest.
newsitem.headline: Turkey attacks Kurd rebels in Iraq despite protest.

text.p: Turkish planes bombed Kurdish rebels fleeing northern Iraq into neighbouring countries on Tuesday as neighbouring Middle Eastern nations increased protests at Turkey's two-week-old military incursion.

"Warplanes rained bombs today and yesterday on terrorists trying to escape from northern Iraq to Iran in the east and Syria in the west," Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency reported military sources as saying.

The agency quoted military officials as saying troops had destroyed eight Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) camps as well as other shelters and stores used by the rebels in the mountains of northern Iraq.

Turkey puts the PKK death toll in the offensive at around 1,750. Rebel sources say around 25 Turkish soldiers are being killed daily. A ban on reporters entering the region made confirmation impossible, but Western diplomats say they believe figures from both sides are exaggerated.
NATO-member Turkey's western allies and regional countries have expressed growing concern over the incursion into a Kurdish enclave protected by the West since the Gulf War ended in 1991.
Iranian President-elect Mohammad Khatami said on Tuesday Tehran opposed the incursion and said it would not help settle differences.

"Our officials have officially launched a protest towards the recent developments...in northern Iraq. The territorial integrity of all countries, including Iraq, has always been a matter of respect to us and we shall defend that," Khatami said.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz accused the United Nations Security Council of being "indifferent" to the Turkish incursion, the official Iraqi news agency said.

"The head of the council and its members have failed so far to take any measure against the invasion except a short statement by the secretary-general," Aziz said in a letter to the chairman of the Security Council carried by the agency.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has condemned the incursion and urged Ankara to pull out its troops.
Jordan urged Turkey to withdraw its troops from the region immediately to avoid a "dangerous escalation", the official Petra news agency quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesman as saying.
Turkish military officials said the offensive would continue until Turkey's Kurdish allies, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) of Massoud Barzani, had total control of northern Iraq.
"The operation will continue until Barzani says 'enough' and the KDP has attained complete authority in northern Iraq," a military source told Anatolian.
More than 10,000 Turkish troops streamed into northern Iraq two weeks ago to pursue PKK rebels who use the region as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
On Monday night, PKK guerrillas killed two villagers and wounded one in a raid on a village in the southeastern Turkish province of Diyarbakir, security officials told Reuters.
A Turkish army official brushed off opposition from Iran, Syria and Iraq to the incursion, saying they supported the PKK.

"The separatist organisation (PKK) has many camps in Iran. The terrorists escaping the operation are going to these camps," the official said. "Syria is certainly a country known to feed and shelter terrorists. Iraq is one of the country's supporting the PKK."
Turkish officials have said Iran, Syria and Iraq were building up military forces on the borders of the Iraqi Kurdish region to help rebels escape.
Turkey mounted a six-week, 35,000-man operation into the Kurdish-held northern Iraqi regions two years ago but failed to achieve its stated aim of clearing the area of PKK.
